superseded_calls.notes: Source sentence: 'Et nulla saltem ab adversae Scholae Doctoribus rejicitur, quam domestici quoque aliqui non impugnent.' English: 'And at least no view is rejected by teachers of the opposing school without some of its own members attacking it too.' The source states 'no view is rejected... unless some domestic ones also do not oppose it' (double negative implying rejection only occurs when some domestic ones DO oppose). English states 'no view is rejected... without some of its own members attacking it too' (rejection only occurs when some domestic ones DO attack). Logical polarity is flipped: source requires domestic non-opposition for rejection to NOT happen; English requires domestic opposition for rejection to happen. This inverts the condition.

The English translation accurately captures the meaning and structure of the single Latin source paragraph, dividing it into two English paragraphs for readability without losing any content or altering agency, negation, or modality.

The source Latin begins 'IX. Quum autem libertas extenditur ad actus necessarios atque immutabiles...' but the English omits the clause 'Quum autem libertas extenditur ad actus necessarios atque immutabiles, fatentur illam latiori significatione sumi;' which translates to 'They admit that when freedom is extended to necessary and unchangeable acts, they acknowledge it is taken in a broader sense.' The English only renders 'They admit that whenever the word is stretched to cover acts that are necessary and unchangeable, it is being used loosely.' which loses the explicit acknowledgment by 'they' (fatentur) and the contrast between broad and strict usage, thus dropping a source clause.

The English translation accurately captures the Latin text, splitting it into two paragraphs for readability while preserving the exact meaning of 'libertas extenditur ad actus necessarios' and 'libertatem vero strictius acceptam'.

English paragraph 1 adds: 'The Reformed who teach that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference toward acting freely admit both points.' This clause has no basis in the Latin source and is an invented addition, violating completeness.

The English translation accurately and completely captures the Latin source paragraph across its two English paragraphs, preserving all theological distinctions, negations, modalities, and agencies regarding the debate on the indifference of the will.
